walkthroughs.body_html:
Alpha: stopped by paper.

Beta: stopped by aluminium.

Gamma: reduced by lead.

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay.

Activity halves too.

Sources: radon, food, cosmic rays, medical, nuclear.

Subtract from measurements.

mcqs.q: What absorber is needed to stop beta radiation?
options: Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
A few millimetres of aluminium (or similar thin metal sheet).
Thick lead — only lead can stop any radiation.
A sheet of paper — beta is only slightly more penetrating than alpha.

mcqs.q: Is radioactive decay periodic — does each nucleus decay at regular intervals?
options: Thick lead — only lead can stop any radiation.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
No — decay is a random process; half-life is a statistical property of a large population.
Yes — each nucleus 'ticks' at intervals of one half-life until it decays.

mcqs.q: Is background radiation always present, even when no source is being studied?
options: No — background radiation only appears near nuclear power stations.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
Yes, but only in cities with old buildings.
Yes — natural sources (rocks, cosmic rays, food) produce a low level of radiation everywhere on Earth.
